case_name: Sushil Kumar Mehrotra v State of Uttar Pradesh
respondent:
State of Uttar Pradesh
Supreme Court of India

1  May  1984
S.L.P. (Cri) No. 972 of 1983 (From the Judgment and Order Dt. 8 March 1983 of the Allahabad High Court in Cr. A. No. 24 of 1977).
The judgment of the Court was delivered by: A. Varadarajan, J.
1. facts: The petitioner Sushil Kumar Mehrotra seeks special leave u/art. 136 of the Constitution to file an appeal against the judgment of the Allahabad High Court (Lucknow Bench) in Criminal Appeal No. 24 of 1977, confirming his conviction by the learned Additional Sessions Judge, Lucknow for offences punishable u/s. 302 read with S. 34 and Section 394, Indian Penal Code, 1860 and the sentence of life imprisonment awarded for each of the offences.
The murder alleged was of the petitioner's mother's sister Urmila, wife of Bhalla, PW 4 in the house of the deceased and PW 4 at about 7.30 p.m. on March 22, 1975.
One of those three persons had a pistol while the other had an open knife and the petitioner had a bag and was wearing only a baniyan and pants and not any shirt.
There was also a blood-stained shirt lying inside the house of the deceased and PW 4.
Autopsy on the body of the deceased disclosed an abrasion on the right frontal area just above the eyebrow and contusion on the lip and multiple abrasions on the face and the neck.
The evidence of PW 6 showed that no investigation was conducted in respect of Sushil Kumar Tandon and Shyam Shukla and no charge-sheet was even filed against them.
There was no direct evidence against the petitioner. The case against the petitioner rested only on circumstantial evidence.
PW 4 had deposed about the earlier visit of the petitioner and his two friends to his house and about their continuing to remain in the house even when he left for his duty at the Railway Station.

The trial court as well as the appellate court found that the circumstantial evidence and identification of the petitioner by PWs 1 to 3 satisfactorily proved the guilt of the petitioner for the offences u/s. 302 read with S. 34 and 394, Indian Penal Code, 1860.
petitioner_arguments: The contention of the petitioner that he was only 15 1/2 years of age at the time of occurrence is a complete afterthought, for no such contention was raised either before the trial court or before the High Court when the appeal was heard or even in the grounds of the special leave petition as originally filed.

The statement of the petitioner made before the trial court u/s. 313 of the Code of Criminal Procedure was that the deceased was his aunt and had no issues and she wanted to adopt him as her son and there was no justification for the petitioner to murder her before she adopted him.

If the petitioner was only 15 1/2 years old at the time of the occurrence and only a little over 18 years of age at the time of trial it is improbable that such a stand would have been taken on behalf of the petitioner and that such an important circumstance that he was a child below 16 years of age under S. 2 (4) of the U.P. Children's Act, 1951 would not have been taken note of by the learned counsel for the petitioner at the time of trial or during the hearing of the appeal in the High Court or while drafting the grounds in the special leave petition as originally filed.
court_reasoning: The contention of the petitioner that he was only 15 1/2 years of age at the time of occurrence is a complete afterthought, for no such contention was raised either before the trial court or before the High Court when the appeal was heard or even in the grounds of the special leave petition as originally filed.

We are satisfied on a perusal of the record that the contention of the petitioner that he was only 15 1/2 years of age at the time of occurrence is a complete afterthought, for no such contention was raised either before the trial court or before the High Court when the appeal was heard or even in the grounds of the special leave petition as originally filed.

Therefore, we find no material on record on the basis of which it could be held that the petitioner was below 16 years of age at the time of occurrence in this case and that S. 27 of the U.P. Children's Act, 1951 was attracted There is no merit.
holding: The special leave petition is dismissed.
